evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with chronic coronary syndrome/stable angina in primary and cardiology care: diagnosis (CT coronary angiography first line), symptom relief, anti-anginal drug sequence, secondary prevention and revascularisation referral. Verified against NICE CG126 (stable angina), CG95 (chest pain diagnosis) and NG238 (lipids); doses and contraindications from US FDA prescribing information. ESC 2024 chronic coronary syndrome guideline and Saudi guidance were not reviewed. Acute coronary syndrome is a separate topic.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 12 Oct 2026.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: ESC 2024 chronic coronary syndrome guideline not reviewed
No Saudi chronic coronary guidance reviewed

pathophysiology.summary: Ischaemic heart disease (coronary artery disease) is myocardial ischaemia from atherosclerotic narrowing of the coronary arteries. Stable angina is predictable chest discomfort on exertion or emotion, relieved by rest or a nitrate within minutes, caused by a fixed stenosis limiting flow when oxygen demand rises.
keyMechanisms: Atherosclerotic plaque narrows the lumen; flow reserve is adequate at rest but insufficient when demand rises (heart rate, BP, contractility) → supply–demand mismatch → angina.
Beta-blockers lower heart rate and contractility; calcium-channel blockers dilate coronaries and reduce afterload; nitrates reduce preload — all reduce demand or improve supply.
Plaque rupture or erosion turns stable disease into an acute coronary syndrome — secondary prevention (antiplatelet, high-intensity statin, BP and risk-factor control) reduces events.
Significant CAD on CT: 70% or more stenosis in a major epicardial segment or 50% or more in the left main (NICE CG95).

symptoms: Constricting chest, neck, shoulder, jaw or arm discomfort, precipitated by exertion and relieved by rest or GTN within about 5 minutes (typical angina: all three features).
Exertional breathlessness (angina equivalent), especially in older people, women and people with diabetes.
physicalSigns: Signs of risk factors or complications: hypertension, xanthelasma, carotid bruits, signs of heart failure, aortic stenosis murmur (alternative cause of angina).
redFlags: Pain at rest, increasing frequency/severity or pain lasting over 15 minutes — possible ACS: call ambulance
Pain persisting 5 minutes after a second GTN dose — emergency (NICE)
Syncope or breathlessness on exertion with ejection systolic murmur (aortic stenosis)
Symptoms uncontrolled on two anti-anginal drugs — consider revascularisation

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Rest pain, crescendo pattern, troponin rise.
Not exertional; reproducible tenderness; reflux symptoms.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Q waves, ST depression, T-wave inversion, LBBB.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: A normal ECG does not exclude CAD; ECG changes with non-anginal pain still warrant CT coronary angiography (CG95).
ruleIn.normalValue: Sinus rhythm, no Q waves or ST-T changes

clinicalManagement.title: Diagnose
actions: Assess pain typicality; ECG; CT coronary angiography first line when angina cannot be excluded clinically (CG95).
Treat as stable angina while awaiting tests if symptoms are typical; consider aspirin until diagnosis (CG95).

clinicalManagement.title: Relieve episodes
actions: Short-acting GTN for treatment and before planned exertion; repeat after 5 minutes; call an ambulance if pain persists 5 minutes after the second dose (CG126).

clinicalManagement.title: Anti-anginal drugs
actions: First line: a beta-blocker or a calcium-channel blocker, chosen by comorbidities and preference; titrate to maximum tolerated dose.
Not controlled: switch to the other or combine — with a beta-blocker use a dihydropyridine CCB (amlodipine, slow-release nifedipine, felodipine).
Beta-blocker and CCB both unsuitable: long-acting nitrate, ivabradine, nicorandil or ranolazine as monotherapy or add-on.
Third drug only if uncontrolled on two and awaiting or unsuitable for revascularisation.

clinicalManagement.title: Secondary prevention
actions: Aspirin 75 mg daily (consider, weighing bleeding risk) (CG126).
Atorvastatin 80 mg (NG238); target LDL 2.0 or non-HDL 2.6 mmol/L or less.
ACE inhibitor if diabetes; treat hypertension; stop smoking; cardiac rehabilitation-style lifestyle support.
No vitamin or fish-oil supplements for angina (CG126).

clinicalManagement.title: Revascularisation
clinicalManagement.timeframe: If symptoms persist on optimal medical therapy
actions: Consider PCI or CABG when symptoms are not controlled on optimal medical treatment (CG126); multidisciplinary heart team decision.

keyPoints: CT coronary angiography first line for suspected angina.
GTN for episodes; ambulance if pain persists after 2 doses.
Beta-blocker or CCB first; combine with a dihydropyridine.
Aspirin 75 mg and atorvastatin 80 mg for secondary prevention.
Refer for revascularisation if uncontrolled on optimal therapy.
pitfalls: Combining a beta-blocker with verapamil or diltiazem.
Missing aortic stenosis as the cause of angina.
Adding a third anti-anginal without considering revascularisation.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Constricting discomfort, triggered by exertion, relieved by rest or GTN within about 5 minutes
70% or more stenosis in a major segment, or 50% or more left main

medicationPlan.note: Drug choice and sequence are from NICE CG126; aspirin 75 mg from CG126 and atorvastatin 80 mg from NG238; other doses and contraindications from US FDA labels. Ivabradine and nicorandil: specialist use (MHRA safety advice noted in CG126). Check SFDA registration, formulary and availability.
